why: Phase 4d converts application SQL -- the Oracle statements embedded in the application rather than in the database. No application codebase exists in this project, so there was nothing to convert and nothing to verify against. These two mapper files carry 25 seeded constructs with known-correct PostgreSQL forms, following the pattern 09_seed_model_tier_plsql.sql set for the PL/SQL model tier: real defects, a published answer key, honestly labelled as seeded.
scope_note: The tables and columns are the real DBMIG_APP ones Phase 1 discovered (CUSTOMER, LOAN, COMM_LOG, PAYMENT_HIST). SQL referencing tables that do not exist could not pass a validate gate, and a phase that cannot be validated proves nothing.

expected_totals.note: A statement may carry several constructs; the MERGE upsert alone carries MERGE, DUAL and SYSDATE. Totals are asserted by scripts/demo-app/verify_appsql.py, not by the phase reporting on itself.

constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: Deleting `FROM DUAL` is mechanical, but inside a MERGE the USING subquery still needs a row source, so the rewrite differs by context.
The sequence name becomes a quoted string, so case folding matters: NEXTVAL on CUSTOMER_SEQ is nextval('customer_seq') on a lower-cased target.
Removed from PostgreSQL entirely. Which table becomes the LEFT side depends on which side carried the (+), and a comma-join with several predicates has to be re-expressed as an explicit join tree.

The ORDER BY must stay inside the subquery or the page contents change. ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY in the same query block, which is why the idiom nests twice -- a converter that flattens it returns different rows.

The operator is identical and the behaviour is not. `NULL || 'x'` is 'x' in Oracle and NULL in PostgreSQL, so a concatenation over a nullable column silently returns NULL where it used to return text.
Direct equivalent; listed because it is the commonest construct in application SQL and belongs in the deterministic tier.

There is no rewrite. Oracle stores '' as NULL; PostgreSQL stores an empty string. Every IS NULL test, unique constraint and NOT NULL column over a column the application writes '' into behaves differently. This is an application redesign, and it is the single most under-estimated difference between the engines.
Mechanical, but DECODE compares NULL equal to NULL and CASE does not, so a DECODE with a NULL search value needs an IS NULL branch.

The format models differ in case handling and padding, and Oracle's MON is NLS_DATE_LANGUAGE-dependent while PostgreSQL's is lc_time-dependent. A wrong format model produces output that looks right in English and breaks elsewhere.

Added 2026-09-17 after the classifier found it and this key had not listed it -- it was folded into APPSQL-009's note instead of carrying its own row. to_date returns a PostgreSQL DATE, which has no time component; where the Oracle value needed its time the rewrite is to_timestamp, so the target column type decides which.
A keyword swap, and genuinely nothing more. Included as a case that must NOT reach the model.

constructs.postgresql: no equivalent; the hint is dropped
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: A hint is a comment, so PostgreSQL ignores it silently rather than failing. Nothing breaks and the plan may regress, which makes this the one construct that must be REPORTED rather than converted -- a dropped hint that nobody saw is a performance incident after cutover.

Which form is correct depends on the target's major version, and the ON CONFLICT form needs a unique constraint to name. PostgreSQL 16 is the target here, so MERGE is available -- but ON CONFLICT is usually the better rewrite and the choice is a judgement.
Oracle DATE has second precision. A bare LOCALTIMESTAMP is microsecond, so a value written by the application never equals a value compared against it.

constructs.postgresql: FOR UPDATE NOWAIT (same syntax, different error)
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: The syntax is accepted. Oracle raises ORA-00054 and PostgreSQL raises SQLSTATE 55P03, so application code catching the Oracle code stops handling lock contention and the failure surfaces as an unhandled exception under load.

constructs.oracle: CONNECT BY / START WITH / PRIOR / LEVEL
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: LEVEL must be synthesised in the recursive term, ORDER SIBLINGS BY has no equivalent, and cycle detection is explicit in PostgreSQL where Oracle offers NOCYCLE.
The ordering moves inside the aggregate call, and LISTAGG's ON OVERFLOW clause has no equivalent -- PostgreSQL has no 4000-byte limit to overflow.
TRUNC is overloaded on number and date in Oracle; PostgreSQL has separate functions, so the rewrite depends on the argument's type.
Oracle returns a fractional month count using a 31-day convention. The PostgreSQL idiom via EXTRACT over an interval returns whole months, so a threshold comparison changes which rows match.
ADD_MONTHS clamps to month end -- 31 Jan plus one month is 28 Feb. The interval form yields 3 March. A loan review date computed either way differs by days.

constructs.postgresql: right() or substring() with computed offset
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: Oracle counts a negative start from the end of the string. PostgreSQL's substring() returns a different result rather than raising, so the defect is silent.

constructs.postgresql: no equivalent with an occurrence argument
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: position() takes no occurrence or start argument. The 4-argument form needs a regexp or a lateral join to reproduce.

constructs.postgresql: no stable equivalent (ctid is not stable)
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: ctid changes on UPDATE and VACUUM. An application that round-trips a ROWID to identify a row must be redesigned around the primary key. No rewrite of the SQL alone is correct.
Direct equivalent, but Oracle's TO_NUMBER tolerates surrounding whitespace that a bare cast rejects.

This is a MyBatis construct, not an Oracle one, and it is here because it is the commonest way an automated converter breaks a mapper: rewriting ${orderBy} to #{orderBy} produces a bound parameter where a column name is needed, and the query fails at runtime rather than at conversion. It is also an injection site the reviewer must flag.

constructs.postgresql: INSERT ... RETURNING, or a DEFAULT nextval column
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: MyBatis handles generated keys differently per engine. The idiomatic PostgreSQL rewrite drops selectKey entirely in favour of RETURNING, which changes the mapper's structure rather than just its SQL.

constructs.oracle: a table or column named ORDER (a PostgreSQL keyword)
constructs.why_not_a_text_swap: Added 2026-09-18 after reading Phase 4c: DBMIG_APP really has a table called ORDER with a column called ORDER, both legal unquoted Oracle identifiers and both PostgreSQL keywords, so convert/ddl.py renames them to order_col and its own note says 'application SQL referencing this name must change'. Nothing was checking that. It is the commonest silent breakage in a heterogeneous migration: the statement still parses on Oracle, so it survives every test until cutover, and then names an object the target does not have. 4d cannot invent the new name -- the rename is 4c's decision -- so the statement is reported with the object and a person applies 4c's mapping.
constructs.cross_phase: convert/ddl.py ident() raises the reserved_word note; only 4d can find the application statements that must follow the rename.

tier_totals.note: Five of 27 constructs have no correct automatic rewrite: empty-string semantics, dropped hints, ROWID round-trips, the MyBatis interpolation case, and an object Phase 4c renamed because Oracle allows a PostgreSQL keyword as an identifier. Eight convert by rule and fourteen need judgement. But the figure to quote is the STATEMENT one, not the construct one: only 2 of 18 statements convert by rule (11%), because a statement carrying even one unhandleable construct is declined whole -- createLoan has three handleable constructs and still declines on selectKey. The construct figure flatters the tooling.
